newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW -- U.S. Aug retail sales up 0.2 pct.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW -- U.S. Aug retail sales up 0.2 pct.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Commerce Department reported August retail sales rose 0.2 percent.
Minus automobiles, sales were also up 0.2 percent.
Economists in a Reuters poll had expected a 0.7-percent rise overall and a 0.4-percent increase excluding cars.

DAVID BLITZER, CHIEF ECONOMIST, STANDARD AND POOR'S CORP: "I think more attention will be paid to retail sales. It came in quite weak. And there will be some people who are trying to place bets that the Fed may not hike rates by 25 basis points."

KEVIN FLANAGAN, VICE PRESIDENT AND ECONOMIST, DEAN WITTER REYNOLDS INC: "(Retail Sales) may have been a little bit more of a surprise -- the weakness that you saw there. Given the back-to-back modest performances, thus far in the third-quarter, meaning July and August, I think you are going to start to hear more and more that the consumer may have pulled back a bit."

PATRICK DIMICK, ECONOMIST, CS FIRST BOSTON: "Retail sales dodged the bullet of upward revisions, which is always a possibility. There could not be a better set of numbers for the bond market. The focus was on CPI, because that would have forced the Fed into action regardless of what retail sales said. Retail only became an item once you cleared the CPI hurdle."
JAMES GLASSMAN, SENIOR MONEY MARKET ECONOMIST AT CHASE SECURITIES INC: "The downward revisions to both June and July make the trajectories weaker for retail sales coming into the late summer.
"Consumer spending went into a stall in the summer. In this particular report the extreme weakness was building materials, food stores grocery stores.

"The revisions still make the consumer look pretty flat in the summer, but that follows a very strong first half. Economists think there should be no debate that Fed should move, but a lot of the economics community would move back to a 50-50 bet."
"It will change the market's expectations, but that's because the Fed hasn't been very clear.
"The reason for tightening would be to avoid a problem next year.

"(The Fed) shoudlnt be distracted by the very favorable inflation trends this year, but they are only human and maybe they would feel awkward explaining the tightening. This will be a real test for them," Glassman concluded.
